lessons.title: Engagement Patterns in Physical Activity and Sport

before.content_html:
What Are Engagement Patterns?

Engagement patterns describe who participates in physical activity, how often, and in which activities. They vary significantly across different social groups — not because of differences in ability, but because of the social, cultural, economic and practical factors that shape people’s lives. Understanding why participation differs between groups is central to this topic, because the goal of sport policy is to remove barriers and make physical activity genuinely accessible to everyone.

Current participation trends in the UK are tracked by several respected bodies. Sport England publishes the Active Lives survey, which measures participation across age groups, sports and regions. National Governing Bodies (NGBs) collect data specific to their own sport. The Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) oversees national sport strategy and funding. Together these sources give a picture of who is active and where the gaps remain.

Factors Affecting Participation: Social and Cultural

Several social and cultural factors shape engagement patterns. Gender remains a significant variable: women and girls historically face barriers including sexism, stereotyping and lower media coverage of women’s sport, which limits the visibility of female role models. When Beth Mead scored a hat-trick at the 2022 UEFA Women’s Euros, grassroots girls’ football registrations rose sharply — evidence of how role models translate directly into participation.

Ethnicity and religion/culture add further dimensions. Race-based discrimination creates hostile environments that deter participation in clubs and competitions. Cultural norms within some communities restrict female participation in mixed-sex sport or in activities where uniform requirements conflict with modesty expectations. Religious observance — prayer schedules, fasting periods, festival commitments — can create scheduling conflicts with training and competition. Coaches and clubs that show flexibility around these factors can significantly improve engagement for these groups.

Age shapes participation across the life course. Young people participate at higher rates when PE is compulsory and sport is embedded in school life. Participation often drops sharply after leaving school as competing demands of work and family life reduce available leisure time. Older adults face different barriers: declining physical capacity, fewer social networks, fewer accessible activities, and negative stereotypes about what older people can or should do. Accessible provision — walking football, seated yoga, aqua aerobics — is critical for sustaining engagement in older age groups.

Key Fact

Sport England, National Governing Bodies (NGBs) and the DCMS are the three main sources of participation data in the UK. Social and cultural barriers include sexism and stereotyping (gender), discrimination (ethnicity), cultural and religious scheduling conflicts, and age-related stereotyping and declining provision for older adults.

Factors Affecting Participation: Economic and Practical

Socio-economic factors cut across all groups. Cost and disposable income determine whether a family can afford club memberships, specialist equipment, coaching fees and travel to competitions. Young people from lower-income households are significantly less likely to participate in organised sport. Free or subsidised community sport programmes are therefore critical to equitable access.

Time and work commitments are a persistent barrier for adults. Working patterns, shift work, childcare and caring responsibilities all compete with leisure time. Women are disproportionately affected by caring commitments, which partly explains lower participation rates among adult women in formal sport. Family influence cuts both ways: children whose parents participate in sport are significantly more likely to be active themselves, because parents model behaviour and provide the practical support — transport, fees, kit — that enables participation.

Education shapes early exposure: schools that offer a diverse range of activities build habits of participation that often persist into adulthood. Opportunity and access depend on whether suitable facilities exist locally. Environment and climate affect participation in outdoor activities — rural communities may lack indoor facilities, while urban areas may have limited green space for field sports. Media coverage and visible role models matter enormously: when a sport receives little media attention, potential participants never encounter it as a realistic option. Role models from under-represented groups signal that a sport is “for people like me.”

People with physical or intellectual disabilities historically face some of the most significant barriers to sport participation. Physical barriers include inaccessible facilities (steps rather than ramps, no hoist equipment in pools), lack of adapted equipment and absence of disability-specific sessions. Attitudinal barriers are often harder to address: negative stereotypes assume that disabled people are not interested in or capable of competitive sport. Dame Sarah Storey’s 17 Paralympic gold medals and the growth of wheelchair basketball as a spectator sport challenge these assumptions directly. Where governing bodies and leisure centres invest in adaptive provision — boccia, sitting volleyball, goalball, deaf-friendly coaching — participation among disabled groups rises.

Strategies to Improve Participation

The OCR specification identifies three strategies that bodies such as Sport England and NGBs use to improve participation. Promotion involves raising awareness of physical activity opportunities through advertising, campaigns and role model endorsements. Sport England’s “This Girl Can” campaign used promotion to target women who felt sport was not for them, directly challenging stereotypes. Provision means creating and maintaining physical activity opportunities: building accessible facilities, funding community sport programmes, training coaches and creating adapted sessions for under-represented groups. Access refers to removing practical barriers that prevent people from taking part even when opportunities exist — subsidising membership costs, providing transport, scheduling sessions at times that suit working parents, and ensuring facilities are physically accessible.

Key Fact

Three strategies to improve participation: Promotion (raising awareness and challenging stereotypes through campaigns and role models), Provision (creating opportunities, facilities and adapted sessions), and Access (removing practical barriers such as cost, transport and scheduling). All three are needed together for sustained change.

Students sometimes treat engagement barriers as isolated, single-cause problems. In reality, a person’s engagement is typically shaped by several factors simultaneously. A woman from a lower-income ethnic minority background in a rural area with caring responsibilities faces overlapping economic (cost), cultural (stereotyping, discrimination), geographical (access) and practical (time) barriers at once. A strong extended-response answer will recognise this overlap — and note that strategies must address multiple factors together, not in isolation, to produce lasting improvements in engagement patterns.

before.exam_tip_html: On a 6 marks — Analyse question about commercialisation, list-style answers score poorly. Each point should follow a three-step structure: state the impact, link it to how it affects a specific group (performer, sport, audience, sponsor), then give a plausible sporting example. On an 8 marks — Evaluate question, you must discuss both positive and negative impacts. A common error is writing only positives or only negatives — OCR’s levels-based mark scheme explicitly rewards a balanced argument. Use a ‘For X… However Y…’ structure and anchor each side to a sporting context. For example: “Sponsorship income allows elite athletes to train full-time [positive]. However, commercial pressure can force athletes to compete while injured to meet contractual obligations [negative].”

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the golden triangle in sport?
A) The three phases of athletic training: strength, endurance and speed
B) The mutually reinforcing relationship between sport, sponsorship and the media
C) The three main types of sports facilities: indoor, outdoor and aquatic
D) The three tiers of sports governance: local, national and international
practice_questions.marks: B) The mutually reinforcing relationship between sport, sponsorship and the media [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'commercialisation' in the context of sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition indicating that sport is treated as a product or business; 1 mark for linking this to financial gain or profit, or to the involvement of sponsors, media or businesses. Example full-mark answer: 'Commercialisation is the process by which sport is treated as a commercial product, with businesses investing in it to generate profit through sponsorship, media rights and merchandise sales.'

practice_questions.text: State two types of sponsorship that a professional sports club might receive.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct types: financial sponsorship (1); clothing and equipment sponsorship (1); facility or venue sponsorship (1). Two answers describing the same type of financial support score only 1 mark.

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the estimated annual broadcast rights income (in millions of pounds) for four sports in the UK.

Sport | Annual broadcast rights income (£m)
Premier League football | 1,650
Rugby Union (Premiership) | 55
Women's Super League | 12
Athletics (UK events) | 8

Using the data in Table 1, interpret what this shows about the relationship between media coverage and commercialisation across these sports.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying the sport with the highest broadcast income (Premier League football, £1,650m); 1 mark for a valid comparison using figures (e.g. Premier League income is over 200 times greater than Women's Super League income of £12m; or athletics earns only £8m compared to rugby's £55m); 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (sports with larger television audiences attract greater broadcast income, which feeds into the golden triangle to attract more sponsorship and commercial partners); 1 mark for a relevant implication (less commercially broadcast sports receive less sponsorship income, leaving them under-resourced; or high broadcast income enables the Premier League to invest heavily in facilities, academies and coaching).

practice_questions.text: Explain two positive impacts and two negative impacts of sponsorship on performers in sport.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark each for any of the following, up to 4 marks total (must cover both positives and negatives for full marks).
Positive: financial security allowing full-time training (1); access to high-quality equipment and coaching (1); increased public profile through media exposure (1).
Negative: pressure to compete while injured to meet commercial obligations (1); loss of control over personal image as a brand ambassador (1); intense media scrutiny of personal life affecting mental wellbeing (1); risk of sudden loss of income if sponsor withdraws (1).

practice_questions.text: A county-level hockey club has recently attracted a regional sports retailer as a kit sponsor. Analyse the impact of this sponsorship arrangement on the club, its players and the sponsoring company.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Discusses impacts on all three parties (club, players and sponsor) with developed points and specific examples. Considers both positive and negative implications for at least two parties. Uses accurate commercial vocabulary (sponsorship, branding, profile, obligations, golden triangle). Continuous analytical prose rather than a list.

Secure: Covers at least two of the three parties with developed points; mostly accurate; some sporting application.

Developing: Relevant points but limited development; may address only one party; minimal sporting context.

Emerging: Basic or vague points; no development; may only state that sponsorship provides money.

Acceptable points: Club gains kit and equipment costs covered and may attract better players (positive); club faces pressure to display sponsor logos prominently or associate with the brand (limitation); players gain professional-quality kit and raised local profile (positive); players may feel obligated to represent the brand positively off the pitch (constraint); sponsor gains brand visibility at matches and on player kit (positive); sponsor risks reputational damage if players behave badly (negative); sponsor reaches a targeted local audience of sport participants (commercial benefit).

practice_questions.text: Identify the category of performance-enhancing drug most likely to be used by a competitive archer wanting to reduce their heart rate during competition.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: beta blockers (1).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'stimulants' in the context of sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that stimulants increase alertness or reduce fatigue; 1 mark for linking this to improved competitive performance or naming a side effect. Example full-mark answer: 'Stimulants are drugs that increase alertness, reduce fatigue and heighten competitiveness, giving performers in high-speed or combat sports a performance advantage, though they are prohibited in competition and carry side effects including elevated heart rate and risk of cardiac arrest.'

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the percentage of tested athletes in three sports who returned a positive test for prohibited substances in an international governing body's annual anti-doping report.

Sport | Positive test rate
Weightlifting | 3.8%
Archery | 1.2%
Athletics | 2.1%

Using the data in Table 1, calculate the difference in positive test rate between weightlifting and archery. Show your working.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct working (3.8% - 1.2%); 1 mark for the correct answer (2.6); 1 mark for the correct unit (percentage points or %). Full-mark answer: '3.8% - 1.2% = 2.6 percentage points. Weightlifting has a positive test rate 2.6 percentage points higher than archery.'

practice_questions.text: Using Table 1 above, interpret what the data shows about PED use across the three sports and suggest one reason why the highest rate appears in weightlifting.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly identifying weightlifting as having the highest positive test rate (3.8%); 1 mark for a valid comparison using figures (e.g. weightlifting's rate is more than three times that of archery at 1.2%); 1 mark for interpreting what this shows (PED misuse is more prevalent in strength-based sports where physical power is a direct determinant of performance); 1 mark for a valid reason linked to the nature of the sport (anabolic steroids benefit power and strength athletes by increasing muscle mass and reducing recovery time, making the potential gain much greater in weightlifting than in precision or technical sports).

practice_questions.text: Explain two reasons why a professional performer might choose to use anabolic steroids, and two negative consequences of this decision.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks (2 reasons + 2 consequences; must cover both for full marks, 1 mark per point).
Reasons: increased muscle mass improving strength and power performance (1); faster recovery from training enabling greater training volume (1); pressure from peers or coaching culture to use substances to keep up with competitors (1); financial incentive of competition success through prize money or sponsorship (1).
Negative consequences: risk of liver damage or cardiovascular disease (1); hormonal disruption affecting secondary sexual characteristics (1); if detected, receives a competition ban, fines and loss of medals (1); permanent reputational damage affecting future career and sponsorship (1).

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old county-level sprinter is told by a senior teammate that 'everyone uses stimulants to get an edge at the top level' and that testing is rarely carried out at county competitions. Evaluate the arguments for and against the sprinter using stimulants, and reach a conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation presenting genuine arguments on both sides. Uses accurate physiological vocabulary (alertness, reduced fatigue, heart rate, side effects). Challenges the 'everyone does it' reasoning with counter-arguments. Reaches a reasoned, balanced conclusion. Consistent sporting application. Arguments are developed, not just listed.

Secure: Covers arguments for and against; mostly accurate physiological understanding; generally balanced; mostly applied to an athletic context; conclusion present.

Developing: Mostly one-sided or acknowledges both sides without developing either; some relevant points but underdeveloped; limited sporting application.

Emerging: Basic statements about drugs being good or bad; no physiological explanation; descriptive rather than evaluative.

Acceptable arguments for: stimulants increase alertness and reduce fatigue, directly improving sprint performance (1); may level the perceived playing field if the sprinter believes others are using them (1); low perceived risk of detection at county level reduces fear of sanction (1).
Arguments against: stimulants carry real health risks including elevated heart rate, anxiety and in extreme cases cardiac arrest - especially dangerous in a young person (1); the 'everyone does it' argument is flawed: many competitors do not use PEDs, so use creates an unfair disadvantage for clean athletes, not a level field (1); if detected at any level, consequences include a ban, loss of results and a permanent record that could affect future opportunities (1); drug use violates the principles of fair competition and the spirit of sport, causing reputational harm even if not detected (1); the teammate's claim is ethically inappropriate - peer pressure of this kind is one of the key reasons young performers are drawn into deviant behaviour, and the sprinter has the right to refuse (1).
Conclusion: stimulant use is both ethically wrong and practically risky; the short-term performance gain is outweighed by health risks, the unreliability of the 'level playing field' argument, and the long-term consequences for the sprinter's career and integrity.

before.exam_tip_html: On a 1 mark — Identify question about a PED, name the category precisely: “anabolic steroids”, “beta blockers” or “stimulants”. For a 3 marks — Describe question about a specific PED, give three distinct pieces of information: what the substance does, which type of performer would use it and why, and one side effect. Avoid repeating the same point in different words. On an 8 marks — Evaluate question about whether PED use can be justified, you must present genuine arguments on both sides. A response that only condemns PED use without engaging with the reasons performers give for using them will be capped at the Developing band. Use a ‘For X… However Y…’ structure anchored to a sporting example on each side. Remember: OCR specifies only three PED categories — no credit for blood doping, EPO or narcotic analgesics on this specification.
before.content_html:
Performance-Enhancing Drugs in Sport

Performance-enhancing drugs (PEDs) are substances that athletes take to improve their physical or psychological output in training or competition. Most PEDs are prohibited by the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and the governing bodies of individual sports. The use of prohibited substances is considered cheating because it undermines the principle of fair competition and often poses serious health risks to the performer. Despite this, doping remains a persistent problem across numerous sports at elite level.

Why Performers Use Drugs

OCR requires students to understand the reasons why sports performers use performance-enhancing drugs. The most fundamental driver is the desire to gain a competitive advantage: in high-level sport, where the difference between winning and losing can be fractions of a second or tiny increments in strength or endurance, a substance that delivers even a marginal performance improvement may be the difference between a gold medal and obscurity. Linked to this is the pressure of financial reward: elite sport is a career, and success brings sponsorship, prize money and media contracts. Where the incentive to win is enormous, the temptation to use any available means is correspondingly strong.

A second cluster of reasons involves cultural and peer pressure. If a performer believes that their competitors are using prohibited substances — creating what they perceive as an uneven playing field — they may feel compelled to use them simply to compete on the same terms. Within some sporting environments, doping may be tacitly encouraged by coaches, management or team culture, making it difficult for an individual to refuse. A win-at-all-costs culture, reinforced by media attention and commercial pressure, can erode the ethical barriers that would otherwise constrain behaviour. Finally, some performers use drugs not to win but simply to recover from injury more quickly, to train harder, or to manage the physical demands of a very high-performance training schedule.

Key Fact

Performers use PEDs to gain a competitive advantage, because of financial incentives, due to peer pressure or a win-at-all-costs culture, or to recover more quickly and train harder. OCR requires knowledge of exactly three PED categories: anabolic steroids, beta blockers and stimulants.

Key Fact

WADA publishes an annually updated prohibited list covering hundreds of substances across every sport. Athletes bear strict liability — a positive test result leads to a ban regardless of whether the performer knew they had taken the substance.

Anabolic Steroids

Anabolic steroids are synthetic hormones that accelerate the development of muscle mass and reduce recovery time between training sessions. They are most commonly associated with power-based sports — such as weightlifting, shot put, sprinting or rugby — where muscle mass is a direct determinant of performance. By allowing performers to train harder and recover faster, anabolic steroids provide a substantial competitive advantage. Side effects include liver damage, cardiovascular disease, hormonal disruption (including effects on secondary sexual characteristics), and in adolescent users, premature closure of growth plates, which can permanently reduce adult height.

Beta Blockers

Beta blockers reduce heart rate, lower muscle tension and decrease blood pressure by blocking the effects of adrenaline. In sports requiring extreme precision — such as archery, shooting or snooker — a reduced heart rate and steadier hand provides a direct performance advantage, as even a small tremor can affect accuracy. Beta blockers are prohibited by WADA in these specific sports because they provide an unfair advantage. Side effects include nausea, weakness and potentially dangerous cardiac problems. They should only be used under medical prescription.

Stimulants

Stimulants are substances that increase alertness, reduce the sensation of fatigue and heighten aggression and competitiveness. They can improve reaction time and allow a performer to sustain high-intensity effort for longer. Sports such as sprint cycling or combat sports, where aggression and alertness are direct performance assets, have seen stimulant misuse. Side effects include elevated heart rate, anxiety, insomnia and in severe cases cardiac arrest. Stimulants are banned in competition by most governing bodies.

Anabolic steroids benefit power and strength athletes (e.g. a shot-putter who needs greater muscle mass and faster recovery). Beta blockers benefit precision performers (e.g. an archer whose accuracy is affected by a raised heart rate under competition pressure). Stimulants benefit high-speed or combat sport athletes (e.g. a sprint cyclist who needs maximum alertness and aggression over a short burst of effort). Matching the PED to the sport type and explaining the mechanism is the key skill tested in 1-mark Identify and 3-mark Describe questions on this topic.

Impact of Drug Use on Performers

The impact of PED use on individual performers is both physical and social. On the physical side, all three PED categories carry significant health risks: liver damage and cardiovascular disease (anabolic steroids), cardiac problems and weakness (beta blockers), and cardiac arrest or insomnia (stimulants). Beyond health, performers who are caught face bans from competition, fines, and the loss of medals and records. Reputational damage can be permanent — a performer’s entire career may be overshadowed by a doping conviction, affecting future coaching roles, sponsorship opportunities and public standing long after retirement.

Impact of Drug Use on Sport Itself

For sport as a whole, high-profile doping scandals damage credibility: if spectators suspect that results are determined by chemistry rather than talent and effort, they lose trust in the sport. This can reduce attendance, television audiences and sponsorship revenue — feeding back through the golden triangle to reduce the resources available to all performers, clean or otherwise. Sport’s value as a positive social model — promoting health, effort and fair competition — is also undermined when doping becomes associated with a discipline. Governing bodies and anti-doping agencies must invest heavily in testing programmes, which diverts resources from development and participation.

Some performers argue that if everyone is doping, using PEDs simply restores a level playing field. This reasoning should be challenged. First, not all athletes dope — those who refuse are placed at a systematic disadvantage. Second, access to the safest and most effective doping protocols depends on resources, meaning wealthier athletes and nations dope more effectively than poorer ones — an inequality within an inequality. Third, normalising PED use accelerates health risks for all performers by creating a race to ever-higher levels of doping. A strong 8-mark answer will recognise this argument, acknowledge why it holds superficial appeal, and then dismantle it with these counter-points.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes a closed skill?
A) A basketball player receiving a bounce pass from a teammate during a fast break
B) A gymnast performing a vault on a consistent, controlled run-up
C) A tennis player returning a serve from an opponent
D) A rugby scrum-half passing after receiving a ball from a maul
practice_questions.marks: B) A gymnast performing a vault on a consistent, controlled run-up [1 mark]. The environment is stable and predictable; the movement can be pre-planned and repeated identically. All other options involve unpredictable, changing environments (open skills).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'open skill' in the context of sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the core idea: a skill performed in an unpredictable or changing environment. 1 mark for development: the performer must adapt their movement continuously to respond to changes in the situation (accept: opponents, teammates, or external conditions change and the performer reacts to them). Do not credit definitions that describe open skills as difficult or unstructured.

practice_questions.text: Describe three characteristics of skilful movement, using a sporting example for each.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for each characteristic correctly described with a brief sporting example (up to 3 marks). Accept any three of: efficiency — no wasted energy or movement, e.g. an elite swimmer using a high elbow pull to maximise propulsion without excess drag (1); pre-determined — the performer has a clear intended outcome before executing, e.g. a netball shooter visualising the arc before releasing (1); co-ordinated — body parts work in correct sequence, e.g. the approach, hip drive and arm action of a javelin throw combining in a timed chain (1); fluent — movement flows smoothly without pausing, e.g. an experienced breaststroke swimmer blending the pull and kick phases seamlessly (1); aesthetic — the movement is pleasing to observe, e.g. a curved finish shot curling into the top corner (1). Maximum 3 marks.

practice_questions.text: A football coach watches a Year-7 pupil attempt a long pass and notices jerky, hesitant movement with wasted arm tension. Explain how this contrasts with the characteristics of skilful movement shown by an elite midfielder.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for identifying weaknesses in the beginner: movement is not fluent (pausing/jerking between sub-routines) (1); energy is wasted through excess muscle tension, so it lacks efficiency (1). Up to 2 marks for linking to characteristics shown by the elite player: the elite midfielder's movement is fluent — phases blend seamlessly (1); it is efficient — only the required muscles fire in the correct sequence, conserving energy (1). Accept references to co-ordinated or pre-determined with appropriate sporting application.

practice_questions.text: A county athletics coach is classifying the discus throw and the 100-metre hurdles on OCR's two skill continua. Analyse the placement of each event on both continua, justifying your answers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Addresses both skills on both continua (four placements total) with clear, definition-based justifications. Discus throw — simple/complex: towards the complex end; requires co-ordination of approach, spin, hip drive, arm swing and release angle, multiple sub-routines demanding simultaneous control (1); open/closed: towards the closed end during competition; the circle is a fixed, controlled environment and the performer initiates when ready, with no opposition interfering (1). Hurdles — simple/complex: more complex than a flat sprint, as the athlete must time the take-off, lead leg clearance and trail leg mechanics for each barrier (1); open/closed: towards the closed end; the hurdles are fixed positions, the track is constant, the environment is predictable (1). Strong responses note that both events are towards the closed end of the environmental continuum but differ on the difficulty continuum. Consistent use of continuum terminology and definitions throughout.

Secure: Correctly places both events on at least three of the four continuum positions, with mostly accurate justifications. May be less precise on one placement.

Developing: Places each event on one continuum only, or gives correct labels without justification. Some continuum terminology used.

Emerging: Names the continua without placing either skill; or confuses the two continua definitions.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old club swimmer competes in both sprint freestyle events and open-water swimming races. Evaluate the view that the two OCR skill continua give a complete and useful picture of how these two activities differ as sporting skills.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation with a range of points on each side, each applied to the swimming scenario, with a clear and justified conclusion. Arguments in support: the two continua do capture key differences — pool sprint freestyle is towards the closed end (predictable lane, no opponents to dodge) but open-water racing sits further open (currents, other competitors' position, turns around buoys vary); the difficulty continuum distinguishes the more complex demands of open-water navigation (multiple environmental stimuli to process) from the more straightforward cyclic arm-pull pattern of pool freestyle; using the continua helps coaches design appropriate training — pool training can be highly repetitive/closed-skill-focused, while open-water prep needs open-skill adaptability drills. Arguments against: two continua cannot fully capture all distinctions between sports; the five characteristics of skilful movement add a dimension the continua miss (e.g. efficiency differences between the two settings); other factors such as fitness level, pacing strategy and tactics are not addressed by skill classification; the placement on a continuum is somewhat subjective and may vary with the specific race conditions. Justified conclusion: the two continua are a useful starting framework for comparing skills but should be used alongside other analytical tools for a complete picture.

Secure: Two or three developed points on each side, mostly applied to the swimming scenario, with a reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Points on both sides but limited development; may focus on one swimmer only; thin sporting application.

Emerging: One-sided or very basic response; little or no sporting application to the scenario.

before.exam_tip_html: On ‘explain’ and ‘analyse’ questions about skill classification, the most common error is stating a classification without justifying it using the continuum definition. Writing “it is an open skill” alone earns nothing — you must say why (e.g. “it is an open skill because the environment is unpredictable; defenders are repositioning and the performer must adapt continuously”). For an 8-mark evaluate question, always address both continua for each skill scenario, provide a justified placement on each, and apply your answer to a named sporting example. A common error is confusing the two continua — remember: simple/complex is about the number of decisions and sub-routines, while open/closed is about environmental predictability. These are separate dimensions and must be justified separately. On the 5-characteristic question, if asked to ‘describe’ three characteristics, don’t just name them — give a brief sporting example of each to access the full marks.

practice_questions.text: Identify one mental preparation technique a penalty taker in football might use in the moments before striking the ball.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any of the following: imagery (1); mental rehearsal (1); selective attention (1); positive thinking (1). Accept brief descriptions that clearly identify one of the four named techniques. Do not credit arousal management, deep breathing or other techniques not on the OCR specification.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'selective attention' in the context of sporting performance.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the core idea: selective attention is the ability to focus on relevant information during performance. 1 mark for the second dimension: blocking out or filtering out irrelevant distractions (such as crowd noise, opponent behaviour or anxiety) that are not useful to the execution of the skill.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a county-level diver could use mental rehearsal to prepare for a new dive in competition.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that mental rehearsal involves running through the skill sequence internally before physical execution (1). 1 mark for describing the process: the diver runs through each phase of the dive in order (approach, hurdle step, take-off, tuck, entry) in real time, from a first-person perspective, picturing successful execution (1). 1 mark for the benefit: rehearsing the movement activates similar motor pathways to physical practice, reinforcing the movement programme and building familiarity without physical effort or injury risk (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain how positive thinking could help a club-level rugby goal kicker maintain performance under pressure during a high-stakes conversion attempt.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that positive thinking involves replacing negative internal thoughts with prepared positive statements (1). 1 mark for the mechanism: negative thoughts (e.g. 'I always miss under pressure') are interrupted by a prepared positive script, redirecting attention from feared outcomes to execution cues (1). 1 mark for application: the kicker uses a statement such as 'I have practised this kick hundreds of times' or 'trust my technique' to maintain focus on the process (1). 1 mark for the outcome: confidence is maintained, muscles remain relaxed, and the execution cues rather than the outcome drive the performance (1).

practice_questions.text: A club-level gymnast is preparing for her first national competition. Her coach suggests she incorporates all four mental preparation techniques into her warm-up routine. Evaluate how effective each technique could be in helping her perform at her best.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation addressing all four techniques, considering both benefits and limitations for this gymnast scenario, with a justified conclusion. Arguments for imagery: creates multi-sensory familiarity with the competitive hall and the routine before physical execution, reducing the novelty of the competitive environment; limitation: requires skill to generate detailed imagery — a performer new to the technique may struggle to produce vivid, stable mental pictures. Arguments for mental rehearsal: activates motor pathways and reinforces the floor routine sequence without physical fatigue; first-competition nerves may cause rehearsal to be rushed or to drift to negative outcomes if not carefully managed. Arguments for selective attention: narrows focus to the floor and the music, filtering out judge presence and crowd noise — critical for a first national appearance; limitation: developing attention control takes time and practice; it cannot be fully acquired the week before competition. Arguments for positive thinking: interrupts performance anxiety and refocuses the gymnast on what she can do; limitation: statements must be believable — hollow reassurance collapses under real pressure. Conclusion: all four techniques contribute and they work best in combination; selective attention and positive thinking are most immediately deployable, while imagery and mental rehearsal require more practice to be fully effective. Consistent sporting application throughout.

Secure: Addresses at least three techniques with mostly developed points on both sides. Mostly applied to the gymnast scenario. Reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Addresses two or three techniques but one-sided (mostly benefits); thin application or limited development.

Emerging: Names one or two techniques; descriptive rather than evaluative; little sporting application.

practice_questions.text: State two ways in which imagery differs from mental rehearsal as mental preparation techniques.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct differences: imagery focuses on vivid multi-sensory experience (feelings, sounds, sights of the performance environment), while mental rehearsal is a structured run-through of the movement sequence (1); imagery creates mental familiarity with the competitive environment and emotional state, while mental rehearsal rehearses the exact procedural movement programme (1); imagery is broader and sensory, while mental rehearsal is procedural and movement-focused (1). Maximum 2 marks; do not credit the same distinction twice.

before.exam_tip_html: On 4-mark explain questions about mental preparation, the most common error is describing a technique without explaining why it works. Writing “the athlete uses imagery to picture themselves succeeding” earns only 1 mark. To earn the full 4, you must also explain the mechanism — “imagery activates similar neural pathways to physical performance, creating a sense of familiarity with the competitive situation and building confidence before the event” — and apply it to the specific scenario in the question. On the 8-mark evaluate question, always ensure you cover all four techniques (or at least three) and that you consider both the benefits and any limitations. OCR’s levels-based mark scheme rewards range, balance and sporting application. A common pitfall is writing only about one technique in depth — that approach will cap your mark in the lower bands. Use a ‘For X... However Y...’ structure for each technique, anchored to a named sporting example.

practice_questions.text: Identify the type of guidance being used when a gymnastics coach physically moves a learner's arms through the correct cartwheel pattern.
practice_questions.marks: Manual guidance [1 mark]. The coach is physically assisting the performer's movement through direct physical contact, moving their body through the correct movement pattern.

practice_questions.text: State two advantages of using visual guidance when coaching a beginner in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for two distinct advantages: it provides a complete mental image of the skill, giving beginners a blueprint of the correct movement pattern they have no prior experience of (1); video can be replayed, paused and slowed down for detailed analysis of each phase of the movement (1); it shows the whole skill in context, which is more meaningful than an abstract verbal description (1); it is easy to understand without requiring the performer to have prior knowledge of the technique (1). Maximum 2 marks; do not credit the same point with different wording.

practice_questions.text: Describe how a swimming coach could use mechanical guidance when teaching a beginner to swim front crawl, and explain one disadvantage of this approach.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for an accurate description of mechanical guidance in this context: the coach uses armbands, a float or a pull buoy to support the swimmer's body position, allowing them to focus on arm technique while the device provides buoyancy (1). 1 mark for identifying a disadvantage: the swimmer may develop dependency on the float or armbands (1). 1 mark for developing the disadvantage: without the aid the swimmer has not learned to manage their own buoyancy, which is a fundamental requirement for independent swimming; when the aid is removed they must still learn this element from scratch (1).

practice_questions.text: Explain why verbal guidance is more effective for an elite javelin thrower than for a beginner attempting the event for the first time. Use your knowledge of how each performer uses memory in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 2 marks for explaining effectiveness for the elite performer: the elite thrower has an established, detailed movement programme stored in long-term memory (1); a single precise verbal cue (e.g. 'release 3 degrees earlier') activates and fine-tunes this existing pattern, translating into a physical adjustment without disrupting the automatic flow of the skill (1). Up to 2 marks for explaining the limitation for the beginner: the beginner has no stored movement programme in long-term memory (1); they cannot translate abstract verbal instructions into co-ordinated physical movement without also seeing or physically experiencing the skill, so verbal guidance alone provides insufficient information for the beginner to perform correctly (1).

practice_questions.text: A county-level athletics coach is deciding which types of guidance to use with two performers: a Year-7 beginner learning the shot put for the first time, and a county-level sixth-form athlete preparing for a regional championship. Analyse how the coach should use guidance differently for each performer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Analyses at least three guidance types across both performers, with clear justifications rooted in stage of learning and the sporting context. Distinguishes between the two performers consistently throughout. Might include: Visual guidance — for the beginner, a live demonstration of the correct put action provides the mental blueprint they lack; for the elite athlete, video analysis of their glide phase or release angle can identify subtle technical faults (1+1). Verbal guidance — limited use for the beginner because they lack an existing movement programme to attach cues to; highly effective for the elite athlete who can translate a brief technical cue ('extend the glide earlier') into a physical adjustment (1+1). Manual guidance — appropriate for the beginner to give the correct kinaesthetic feel for the stance and wrist position; inappropriate for the elite athlete as it disrupts the automatic motor programme they have developed over years (1+1). Mechanical guidance — a lighter shot or a marked circle could constrain the beginner's practice safely; elite athletes rarely need mechanical guidance for this event. Consistently evaluates rather than just listing.

Secure: Three guidance types discussed with mostly accurate justification. Distinguishes between performers on at least two types.

Developing: Two guidance types with some justification; less clear on why the distinction between beginner and elite exists.

Emerging: One or two types named with little justification; may not distinguish between performers.

practice_questions.text: A 16-year-old club trampolinist is learning a new double somersault. Her coach uses a safety harness during the initial practice sessions. Evaluate whether mechanical guidance is always the most appropriate form of guidance when teaching new acrobatic skills, referring to both its benefits and limitations.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A balanced, well-developed evaluation with a range of points on both sides, consistently applied to the trampolinist scenario and/or other acrobatic sporting examples, with a justified conclusion. Arguments in support of mechanical guidance: the safety harness allows the athlete to experience the correct rotation without risk of injury; the physical sensation from being supported through the skill provides information about body position that verbal description could not convey; it builds confidence so the performer is not held back by fear; it prevents the reinforcement of incorrect patterns by constraining the movement. Arguments against / limitations: over-reliance on the harness creates dependency — the trampolinist may fail to develop the internal body control needed to perform unsupported; the harness slightly alters the feel of the rotation so adjustment is still required when performing without it; other guidance types may be more effective in combination, such as verbal cues ('tuck tighter') and video analysis of unsupported attempts; for acrobatic skills at a lower danger level, visual or manual guidance may be equally effective without the dependency risk; mechanical guidance requires specialised equipment not always available in community settings. Justified conclusion: mechanical guidance is most appropriate in high-risk acrobatic skills during the early learning phase but should be progressively withdrawn as competence develops, combined with verbal and visual guidance for complete skill acquisition.

Secure: Two or three developed points on each side, mostly applied to the trampolinist scenario, with a reasonable conclusion.

Developing: Points on both sides but underdeveloped; sporting context present but thin or predominantly one-sided.

Emerging: Basic response; may list guidance types without evaluating mechanical guidance specifically.

before.exam_tip_html: On 6-mark analyse questions about guidance, the most effective structure is: name the guidance type → explain its key feature → link it specifically to either a beginner or elite performer with a sporting example → justify why it suits that performer level. A common error is saying “visual guidance is good for beginners” without explaining why (beginners have no stored movement pattern to draw on, so seeing the skill demonstrated provides the mental blueprint they need). On the 8-mark evaluate question, always address both benefits and limitations of each guidance type, applying your points to the scenario. Read the scenario carefully — if the question specifies a beginner, the examiner wants to see why, for example, verbal guidance alone would be insufficient. OCR’s levels-based mark scheme rewards range of guidance types discussed, balance (benefits and limitations), and consistent sporting application throughout.

practice_questions.text: Identify which type of feedback comes from within the performer's own body.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: intrinsic feedback (accept internal feedback).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'knowledge of performance'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that knowledge of performance is feedback about the quality or technique of a movement (not the outcome). 1 mark for development: it tells the performer what to correct in their technique rather than simply whether they succeeded or failed; or gives a sporting example (e.g. a coach telling a high jumper their Fosbury flop arch needs to be more pronounced is knowledge of performance).

practice_questions.text: State two sources of extrinsic feedback available to a performer in sport.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark each for any two distinct sources from: a coach or teacher giving verbal instructions; a teammate's comments; video analysis or video replay; heart rate monitor or performance data; scoreboard or result display; crowd reaction. Both answers must be qualitatively different sources to earn 2 marks.

practice_questions.text: Describe how knowledge of results and knowledge of performance each help an athlete improve. Use a sporting example in your answer.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining knowledge of results: information about the outcome (score, time, distance) that tells the performer whether they succeeded or not, providing motivation. 1 mark for explaining knowledge of performance: information about the quality of the movement or technique used, pointing to what specifically needs to change. 1 mark for a relevant sporting example illustrating either or both (e.g. a swimmer learning their race time is 0.4 seconds slower than their personal best is KR; being told their tumble-turn is losing them 0.3 seconds is KP).

practice_questions.text: Explain why positive feedback is particularly important for beginner performers in physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining positive feedback as information that tells the performer what they did correctly. 1 mark for explaining that it reinforces the correct movement pattern in memory, making repetition more likely. 1 mark for linking to the beginner context: beginners make frequent errors and their confidence and motivation can be fragile, so reinforcing what is right encourages continued participation. 1 mark for a specific sporting example or further development (e.g. a beginner basketball player is told 'your shooting stance is perfect' — this confirms a technique she should repeat and helps her build a reliable kinaesthetic reference point).

practice_questions.text: A junior badminton coach works with two groups: a Year 7 beginners' class learning the overhead clear for the first time, and a county under-16 squad preparing for a regional tournament. Evaluate how the coach should differ in the type and focus of feedback given to each group, and which approach is more likely to produce lasting improvement.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): identifies and explains at least two contrasting feedback strategies for each group, linking each strategy to a specific reason grounded in the developmental difference between beginners and experienced performers. For beginners: positive feedback to build confidence; extrinsic feedback because intrinsic awareness is unreliable; knowledge of results as it is simple to understand; overloading with KP can confuse and demotivate. For the county squad: knowledge of performance to address fine technical detail; negative feedback welcomed at this level; well-developed intrinsic feedback can be trusted to supplement coaching. Reaches a balanced, reasoned conclusion about which approach produces more lasting improvement (e.g. KP + trusted intrinsic = deeper learning for elite, but positive/extrinsic = greater long-term retention for beginners if it keeps them engaged). Sustained sporting application throughout.

Secure (5-6 marks): identifies appropriate feedback for each group with explanation; at least one named feedback type per group; sporting context present but may be brief; conclusion present.

Developing (3-4 marks): makes relevant points about beginners needing simpler or more encouraging feedback; development limited; sporting application minimal or absent; one-sided argument.

Emerging (1-2 marks): basic points only (e.g. 'give more positive feedback to beginners'); no sporting application; no balance.

before.exam_tip_html: On a 2 marks — Define question, you need a precise one-sentence definition. “Positive feedback is good feedback” earns nothing — you must specify what it does (reinforces correct actions) and when it is most effective (for beginners). For a 4 marks — Explain question, give the definition (1 mark), explain the mechanism (1 mark), add the sporting example (1 mark), then link to the level of performer (1 mark). A very common error on feedback questions is confusing intrinsic/extrinsic (the source) with positive/negative (the tone) — these are separate dimensions and should never be swapped. On an 8 marks — Evaluate question about feedback types, avoid writing only about one performer level. The mark scheme rewards a balanced argument: positive feedback for beginners (with reasons), knowledge of performance for elite performers (with reasons), then a reasoned conclusion about which approach is more effective and why.

before.content_html:
Defining Health, Fitness and Wellbeing

Three terms sit at the heart of this topic, and OCR expects you to define each precisely. Health is defined by the World Health Organisation as a state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing — not merely the absence of disease. A person can be healthy without being a high-level athlete, and an athlete can be medically fit yet psychologically or socially struggling. True health is multi-dimensional.

Fitness refers to the ability to meet the physical demands placed upon the body. A marathon runner is fit for her event; a weightlifter is fit for his. Fitness is always relative to the activity — there is no single universal measure. Wellbeing is the broader sense of being in a positive state — feeling satisfied, purposeful and capable across physical, emotional and social dimensions. Physical activity contributes to all three simultaneously, which is why it is one of the most powerful public health tools available.

Key Fact

OCR requires three distinct definitions: health (complete physical, mental and social wellbeing), fitness (ability to meet the demands of the environment) and wellbeing (positive state across physical, emotional and social dimensions). These are not the same thing — you can be fit but unhealthy, or healthy but not at peak fitness.

Physical Benefits of Participation

Regular physical activity produces a wide range of physical health benefits, many of which directly reduce the risk of the most serious long-term diseases. The OCR specification names seven physical outcomes you must know: reduced risk of coronary heart disease (CHD), improved blood pressure control, increased bone density, reduced risk of obesity, reduced risk of Type 2 diabetes, improved posture, and improved overall fitness.

Coronary heart disease: regular aerobic exercise strengthens the heart muscle, increases stroke volume and improves the elasticity of blood vessels. These adaptations reduce the risk of fatty deposits narrowing the coronary arteries. Over a lifetime of regular activity, the risk of a fatal heart attack is significantly reduced. Dame Sarah Storey, for example, has maintained exceptional cardiovascular health through decades of competitive cycling.

Blood pressure: regular activity keeps blood vessel walls flexible and reduces the resting demands on the heart, helping to maintain blood pressure within a healthy range. Hypertension (high blood pressure) is a major risk factor for stroke and kidney disease, and inactivity is one of its primary causes.

Bone density and posture: weight-bearing exercise — running, gymnastics, team sport — stimulates bone remodelling, maintaining or increasing bone density and reducing the long-term risk of osteoporosis. Good muscular strength and balanced muscle development also support healthy posture, reducing the back pain and joint problems that arise from prolonged sitting or muscular imbalance.

Obesity and Type 2 diabetes: regular exercise burns energy and maintains muscle mass, supporting a healthy body composition and preventing obesity. Physical activity also improves the body’s sensitivity to insulin, meaning blood glucose is regulated more efficiently. Both obesity and Type 2 diabetes are strongly associated with inactivity, and both significantly increase the risk of further cardiovascular and metabolic disease.

Emotional Benefits of Participation

OCR specifically names three emotional benefits: improved self-esteem and confidence, better stress management, and positive body image. These are not optional extras — they carry equal mark-scheme weight to physical benefits in extended-response questions.

Self-esteem and confidence: achieving a personal best, mastering a new skill or winning a competition builds self-esteem. The process of setting a goal, training towards it and succeeding creates a sense of personal effectiveness that transfers into other areas of life. For young people in particular, sporting achievement can become a foundation for confidence in school, relationships and future careers.

Stress management: moderate to vigorous exercise triggers the release of serotonin, a neurotransmitter linked to feelings of calm and happiness, and endorphins, natural pain-relieving chemicals that produce a sense of euphoria. The neurological effect is a measurable reduction in perceived stress and anxiety. Regular exercisers show lower baseline cortisol (the stress hormone) levels and a faster physiological return to calm after stressful events.

Body image: physical activity improves body composition and physical capability, both of which contribute to a more positive body image. This is particularly significant for adolescents, for whom body image is a major determinant of self-worth. Sport provides an experience of the body as something capable and powerful, rather than something purely aesthetic.

Stress is the body’s physiological response to a perceived threat or challenge. When stressed, the hypothalamus activates the adrenal glands to release adrenaline and cortisol. These hormones raise heart rate, blood pressure and blood glucose, preparing the body for action. Chronically elevated stress hormones damage the cardiovascular system, suppress immunity and impair sleep.

Exercise provides the body with a legitimate outlet for this physiological state. A run or a football training session allows the body to use the elevated heart rate and glucose productively. After exercise, serotonin and endorphin levels remain elevated for several hours, creating a period of improved mood and reduced anxiety. Over time, regular exercisers show lower baseline cortisol levels. This is why physical activity is increasingly recommended by mental health professionals as a first-line intervention for mild anxiety.

Social Benefits of Participation

OCR names three social benefits: the development of friendship, a sense of belonging to a group, and the reduction of loneliness. These are genuine, evidenced outcomes of regular participation and are especially important for specific age groups.

Team sport and group exercise demand cooperation and communication. Playing in a netball team, a rowing eight or a football squad requires trust, shared responsibility and collective problem-solving. These interpersonal skills transfer directly to workplaces and communities. For children and young people, regular team sport is one of the most effective ways of developing the social skills that underpin healthy adult relationships.

Participation also creates structured social contexts where friendships form more easily. For individuals who are isolated — whether through disability, life transitions or mental health difficulties — joining a sports club can directly address loneliness. The shared purpose and regular contact of a club or team provide exactly the conditions in which new social bonds develop. For older adults, group exercise classes and walking clubs perform the same function, reducing social isolation and the health consequences that accompany it.

OCR explicitly requires you to “apply the above to different age groups”. This means you should be able to discuss how the benefits differ across children, young people, adults and older adults. For children: skill development, bone density, socialisation through team sport, building lifelong habits. For young people: stress management, body image, self-esteem, social belonging. For adults: CHD prevention, stress relief, maintaining healthy weight, social connection. For older adults: bone density maintenance (reducing osteoporosis risk), managing Type 2 diabetes, reducing loneliness, maintaining mobility and posture. In an extended-response question, referencing a specific age group with an example will push an answer from Secure to Mastering.

Key Fact

OCR’s named physical benefits: reduced CHD, improved blood pressure, increased bone density, reduced obesity risk, reduced Type 2 diabetes risk, improved posture, improved fitness. Emotional benefits: self-esteem/confidence, stress management, positive body image. Social benefits: friendship, belonging to a group, reduced loneliness. All 13 outcomes are examinable.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Physical activity produces seven named physical health benefits (including CHD prevention, improved bone density, reduced obesity and Type 2 diabetes risk) alongside three emotional benefits (self-esteem, stress management, body image) and three social benefits (friendship, belonging, reduced loneliness).
  • The three dimensions are interconnected: improved physical health supports positive emotional wellbeing, and social participation through sport reinforces both. Addressing all three in exam answers is essential for higher marks.
  • OCR expects you to apply benefits to specific age groups: bone density matters most for children and older adults; stress management is especially relevant for young people; loneliness reduction is particularly significant for older adults.

practice_questions.text: Identify one emotional benefit of regular participation in physical activity.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for any one of: improved self-esteem or confidence; better stress management; more positive body image. Accept precise or descriptive answers.

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'wellbeing'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for a basic definition: a positive state across physical, emotional and social dimensions / feeling satisfied and capable. 1 mark for development: includes both the absence of illness and the presence of positive functioning across all three health dimensions; or gives an example distinguishing wellbeing from mere fitness (e.g. a person can be physically fit yet have poor emotional wellbeing if they suffer from anxiety or low self-esteem).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows participation rates and self-reported wellbeing scores for three groups of adults at a local sports centre.

Group | Weeks of exercise per year | Mean wellbeing score (out of 10)
A (0–5 weeks) | 3 weeks | 4.7
B (20–30 weeks) | 25 weeks | 6.9
C (40+ weeks) | 48 weeks | 8.2

Calculate the difference in mean wellbeing score between Group A and Group C, and suggest what this tells us about the relationship between exercise and wellbeing.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correct calculation: 8.2 - 4.7 = 3.5 points (accept 3.5). 1 mark for showing working and stating the unit (points on the wellbeing scale). 1 mark for a valid inference: the 3.5-point difference in wellbeing scores suggests that higher levels of regular exercise are associated with substantially greater wellbeing, indicating a positive relationship between frequency of participation and wellbeing.

practice_questions.text:
Table 2 shows the bone density measurements (g/cm²) of two groups of 65-year-old women: those who have exercised regularly for 20 years and those who have not.

Group | Mean bone density (g/cm²)
Active (regular exercise) | 1.08
Inactive (little or no exercise) | 0.79

Interpret what the data shows about the effect of regular exercise on bone density in older women.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that active women have higher mean bone density than inactive women (1.08 vs 0.79 g/cm²). 1 mark for quoting both figures to support the comparison. 1 mark for explaining the mechanism: weight-bearing exercise stimulates bone remodelling, maintaining or increasing density over time. 1 mark for the health implication: the 0.29 g/cm² difference suggests regular exercise significantly reduces the risk of osteoporosis and fractures in older adults.

practice_questions.text: A health promotion officer argues that regular physical activity is the single most important factor in improving the wellbeing of older adults aged 65 and over. Evaluate this claim, considering physical, emotional and social wellbeing benefits.

Mastering (7-8 marks): presents a balanced, sustained evaluation with points across all three wellbeing dimensions applied specifically to older adults; argues the case for physical activity (CHD prevention, bone density maintenance, reduced Type 2 diabetes risk, stress reduction, reduced loneliness through group exercise); presents a counter-argument with development (diet, social support networks, healthcare access also contribute to wellbeing; not all older adults can participate in exercise due to disability or chronic illness; some emotional wellbeing issues require professional intervention beyond exercise); reaches a justified conclusion about whether physical activity is the single most important factor. before.content_html:
What Is a Sedentary Lifestyle?

A sedentary lifestyle is one defined by prolonged physical inactivity. The word “sedentary” comes from the Latin for “sitting”, and that is its defining feature: large portions of waking hours spent sitting or lying down, with minimal structured exercise. Modern technology has made sedentary living increasingly easy — screen-based entertainment, desk-based work and motorised transport can combine to mean that some individuals complete fewer than 2,000 steps a day. The Health Survey for England consistently shows that a significant proportion of adults fail to meet the recommended 150 minutes of moderate activity per week.

The consequences of a sedentary lifestyle are cumulative and wide-ranging. They span physical health (weight gain, disease), emotional health (poor self-esteem) and social health (loneliness). Understanding these consequences as distinct but interconnected categories is important for exam answers and for appreciating why public health campaigns consistently promote active living.

Key Fact

The six key consequences of a sedentary lifestyle on OCR are: obesity, coronary heart disease (CHD), Type 2 diabetes, hypertension, low self-esteem and loneliness. Each one is examinable as a named consequence, and each should be linked to the mechanism by which inactivity causes it.

Physical Consequences of Inactivity

Obesity: without regular physical activity to burn energy, intake consistently exceeds expenditure and the surplus is stored as body fat. Obesity is defined as excess body fat accumulation sufficient to adversely affect health, typically measured by a BMI over 30. Once present, obesity creates a secondary cascade — it limits mobility, which makes further activity harder, reinforcing the sedentary cycle. Unused saturated fat also accumulates in blood vessel walls, contributing to atherosclerosis (artery narrowing).

Coronary heart disease: a sedentary heart is a weaker, less efficient heart. Without the regular challenge of aerobic exercise, the heart muscle does not strengthen and blood vessels lose elasticity. Fatty deposits accumulate in the coronary arteries, progressively narrowing them. If a coronary artery becomes blocked, the result is a heart attack. Physical inactivity is one of the most modifiable risk factors for CHD.

Hypertension: Hypertension (high blood pressure) is strongly associated with physical inactivity. Without regular exercise to strengthen blood vessel walls and maintain their flexibility, resting blood pressure tends to rise. Hypertension damages arterial walls over time, increasing the risk of stroke, kidney disease and further cardiovascular damage.

Type 2 diabetes: physical inactivity reduces the body’s sensitivity to insulin, the hormone that regulates blood glucose. When cells become resistant to insulin, blood glucose remains persistently elevated. Over time this develops into Type 2 diabetes, which carries serious long-term complications including nerve damage, vision problems and cardiovascular disease. Regular exercise improves insulin sensitivity, which is why physical activity is a primary recommendation for preventing and managing Type 2 diabetes.

The physical consequences of a sedentary lifestyle do not operate independently — they form a self-reinforcing cascade. Inactivity leads to weight gain and obesity. Obesity increases blood pressure (hypertension) and worsens insulin resistance (Type 2 diabetes). Hypertension and fatty deposits from obesity narrow the coronary arteries, raising CHD risk. Meanwhile, low fitness levels make exercise feel difficult, reinforcing the sedentary behaviour. Understanding this cascade as an interconnected chain — rather than a list of separate conditions — will help you write more analytical extended-response answers.

Emotional and Social Consequences of Inactivity

Low self-esteem: physical inactivity is associated with weight gain, reduced self-efficacy and a more negative physical self-image. Self-esteem — one’s sense of personal worth — is strongly linked to how people perceive their own bodies and capabilities. Individuals who are inactive may lose confidence in physical settings, withdraw from sport and social activity, and develop a negative cycle in which low confidence further reduces the motivation to become active.

Loneliness: physical activity is a major vehicle for social interaction. Team sport, gym classes, recreational clubs and even informal park runs all provide structured opportunities for social contact. A sedentary individual who is no longer engaging in these activities loses a significant source of social connection. Over time, reduced social contact leads to loneliness, which itself has documented negative effects on both mental and physical health — including increased blood pressure, poorer immune function and a higher risk of depression.

A sedentary lifestyle is not inevitable — it is a behavioural pattern shaped by environment, habit and access. Strategies to combat it include: increasing active transport (walking or cycling to school/work), taking regular breaks from desk-based work to stand or move, joining a local sports club, and using activity-tracking technology to set daily step or movement goals. At a societal level, urban planning (safe cycle lanes, green spaces, accessible sports facilities) and workplace wellness programmes directly address the structural drivers of inactivity. OCR may ask you to apply these strategies in context, linking them to the named consequences they prevent.

Key Fact

For exam answers: every named consequence must be linked to its mechanism. Obesity = energy surplus stored as fat. CHD = arterial narrowing from fat accumulation + weakened heart. Hypertension = loss of arterial elasticity and flexibility. Type 2 diabetes = reduced insulin sensitivity. Low self-esteem = negative body image + withdrawal from activity. Loneliness = reduced social contact from inactivity.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A sedentary lifestyle is characterised by prolonged physical inactivity and causes six named consequences on OCR: obesity, coronary heart disease, hypertension, Type 2 diabetes, low self-esteem and loneliness — spanning physical, emotional and social health.
  • The physical consequences form an interconnected cascade: inactivity leads to obesity, which drives up blood pressure and worsens insulin resistance, together raising the risk of CHD and Type 2 diabetes.
  • The emotional and social consequences reinforce the physical ones: low self-esteem reduces motivation to exercise, and loneliness removes the social drivers that keep many people active, sustaining the sedentary cycle.
