practice_questions.text: Identify the macronutrient that the body uses as its main and preferred energy source for all types of exercise.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for: carbohydrate (accept carbs, glucose or glycogen if clearly referring to the macronutrient).

practice_questions.text: Define the term 'balanced diet'.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for the basic definition: a diet containing the correct proportions of all the nutrients the body needs. 1 mark for development: states the seven components (carbohydrates, protein, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre, water); or states the approximate proportions (55-60% carbohydrate, 25-30% fat, 15-20% protein); or gives a sporting example (e.g. an endurance runner needs a higher carbohydrate proportion than a sedentary individual to fuel long training runs).

practice_questions.text:
Table 1 shows the daily macronutrient breakdown of two club-level swimmers during a training week.

Swimmer | Total daily energy | % from carbohydrate | % from protein | % from fat
Aisha | 2,800 kcal | 57% | 18% | 25%
Ben | 2,800 kcal | 44% | 22% | 34%

Using the data, identify which swimmer has a macronutrient balance within the recommended ranges for a balanced diet, and calculate the amount of energy Ben obtains from fat each day.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying Aisha as within balanced-diet ranges: carbohydrate 57% (within 55-60%), protein 18% (within 15-20%), fat 25% (within 25-30%). Ben is outside range (44% carbohydrate is below 55% minimum; 34% fat exceeds 30% maximum). 1 mark for correct calculation: 2,800 x 0.34 = 952 kcal from fat. 1 mark for stating the unit (kcal) and confirming Ben's fat intake exceeds the recommended maximum of 30%.

practice_questions.text:
Table 2 shows heart rate data for two players during the final 20 minutes of a 90-minute football match played in hot conditions. Player A drank water at half-time; Player B drank nothing during the match.

Time | Player A heart rate (bpm) | Player B heart rate (bpm)
70 min | 148 | 163
80 min | 151 | 172
90 min | 149 | 181

Interpret what the data shows about the effect of dehydration on Player B's heart rate, and explain why this change occurred.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for identifying that Player B's heart rate is consistently higher than Player A's across all three time points (163 vs 148 at 70 min, rising to 181 vs 149 at 90 min). 1 mark for quoting specific figures to support the comparison. 1 mark for linking the rising heart rate to dehydration increasing blood viscosity (thicker blood). 1 mark for explaining the mechanism: the heart must beat faster to maintain adequate blood flow to working muscles when blood is thicker, accelerating fatigue and performance decline in the final stages of the match.

practice_questions.text: Explain how an adequate intake of carbohydrate and protein would help a county-level rower prepare for and recover from a five-day intensive training camp.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for explaining carbohydrate's role in preparation: stored as glycogen in muscles and liver, used as the primary fuel during high-intensity rowing training; adequate carbohydrate ensures glycogen stores are full before each session. 1 mark for explaining carbohydrate's role during the camp: replenishing glycogen stores after each session maintains energy availability for subsequent sessions across the five days. 1 mark for explaining protein's role in recovery: muscle fibres are broken down during intense rowing training; protein provides the amino acids needed for repair and adaptation (hypertrophy). 1 mark for a link to performance: insufficient protein slows repair, leaving the rower fatigued and limiting the training adaptations the camp is designed to produce.

practice_questions.text: A 17-year-old club-level long-distance runner is preparing for her first half-marathon. Her coach has recommended she follow a carefully planned diet for the six weeks before the race. Evaluate the extent to which carbohydrate, protein and hydration are each important to her preparation and race performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7-8 marks): presents a balanced evaluation of all three nutritional factors applied specifically to a long-distance runner preparing for a half-marathon; argues the case for carbohydrate (primary fuel, glycogen loading in final days, sustained energy during the 90+ minute race); argues the case for protein (muscle repair across the six-week training block, limiting injury and supporting adaptation); argues the case for hydration (dehydration raises heart rate and blood viscosity, slows reactions, causes muscle cramps, particularly dangerous in a long-duration event); evaluates relative importance with justification (e.g. carbohydrate is arguably most critical on race day because glycogen depletion is the primary cause of 'hitting the wall'; however, without adequate protein across the training block there would be insufficient muscle adaptation to compete); at least one developed counter-argument; sporting application sustained throughout.

Secure (5-6 marks): covers all three factors with explanation; links to the long-distance running context mostly present; some evaluation of relative importance; conclusion present.

Developing (3-4 marks): covers two factors accurately; links to the athlete context limited; limited evaluation; conclusion may be present but not fully justified.

Emerging (1-2 marks): one or two basic accurate points about nutrition or hydration with little sporting application or evaluation.

before.exam_tip_html: On a 3 marks — Calculate from Data question involving nutrition percentages, always show your working, state the unit (%), and present a clear final answer. For example: if asked what percentage of a 3,000 kcal diet should come from protein at the minimum recommended level, the working is 3,000 × 0.15 = 450 kcal. Missing the unit drops a mark. On a 4 marks — Interpret Data question, quoting figures without explaining what they mean earns partial credit only. Always make a comparison, quote at least one figure, then explain the sporting implication. For an 8 marks — Evaluate question about diet and performance, avoid listing nutrients in isolation. Structure your answer around the demands of the specific sport or performer, then link each nutrient to how it meets those demands — or what happens if it is insufficient. A counter-argument (e.g. too much protein without adequate carbohydrate will not improve performance) earns marks in the upper bands.
before.content_html:
Energy Use in Sport and Exercise

Everything the body does — breathing, thinking, sprinting, lifting — requires energy. That energy comes entirely from the food we eat and is derived from a combination of macronutrients. The amount of energy an individual needs depends on several factors: age, gender, body size and, critically for athletes, the amount and intensity of exercise performed. A 16-year-old county-level swimmer training twice a day will have far greater energy needs than a sedentary adult of the same age and size.

OCR focuses on energy use — understanding how the body uses different nutrients as fuel — rather than precise calorie calculations. The key principle is matching food intake to energy demand: an athlete needs to consume enough of the right foods to fuel training, support recovery and maintain a healthy body composition.

Key Fact

An individual’s daily energy requirement is affected by age, gender, body size and energy expenditure (exercise levels). Athletes and highly active individuals need significantly more energy than sedentary people of the same age and gender. Energy balance — intake matching expenditure — is the key principle for maintaining a healthy body composition.

The Balanced Diet: Seven Components

A balanced diet does not mean eating equal amounts of everything. It means eating the right proportions of different food types to supply the body with all the nutrients it needs. OCR requires knowledge of seven components: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, minerals, vitamins, fibre and water. No single food provides every nutrient — variety is essential. The approximate proportions for macronutrients in a balanced diet are: 55–60% carbohydrate, 25–30% fat, and 15–20% protein.

Macronutrients: Carbohydrate, Fat and Protein

Carbohydrate is the primary and preferred fuel for all types of exercise, regardless of intensity. Whether a performer is jogging at a comfortable pace or sprinting at maximum effort, carbohydrates are the first fuel the body calls upon. They are broken down into glucose, which is either used immediately or stored as glycogen in the muscles and liver for use during exercise. Elite distance runners and cyclists often practise ‘glycogen loading’ — consuming carbohydrate-rich meals in the days before an event to maximise glycogen stores. Dina Asher-Smith, for example, works carefully with nutritionists to ensure her glycogen stores are fully loaded before major championships.

Fat provides more energy per gram than carbohydrate, but it can only be used efficiently as a fuel source at low intensity — for example, during a slow, steady-state walk or easy cycle ride. When exercise intensity increases, the body switches back to carbohydrate because fat metabolism is too slow to meet the energy demand. Fat also has important non-energy roles: it insulates the body, protects vital organs, and acts as a carrier for fat-soluble vitamins (A, D, E and K).

Protein is not a primary energy source. Its main role is the growth and repair of muscle tissue — essential after heavy training when muscle fibres have been broken down by the work they have done. Adam Peaty follows a protein-rich recovery plan after intense pool sessions to support muscle repair and adaptation. Consuming insufficient protein slows recovery and limits the muscle adaptations that training is designed to produce.

Key Fact

A balanced diet is approximately 55–60% carbohydrate (main energy source), 25–30% fat (energy at low intensity; insulation; vitamin carrier), 15–20% protein (growth and repair). Carbohydrate is the body’s preferred fuel at all exercise intensities.

Micronutrients: Vitamins, Minerals and Fibre

Vitamins and minerals do not supply energy directly, but they are essential for the efficient working of all body systems. Vitamins support processes from immune function (vitamin C) to bone metabolism (vitamin D); minerals such as calcium are vital for bone density and muscle contraction, while iron is essential for oxygen transport in the blood via haemoglobin. A diet lacking variety will typically be deficient in vitamins and minerals even if its total energy looks adequate.

Fibre is the indigestible component of plant-based foods — found in fruit, vegetables, wholegrain cereals and legumes. Its primary role is to support healthy digestion by adding bulk to stools and maintaining regular bowel function. Fibre also helps regulate blood glucose levels after meals by slowing the absorption of sugar, which is particularly important for athletes trying to maintain stable energy levels across a training day.

OCR does not require you to name specific vitamin or mineral requirements for athletes. However, the general principle is that athletes engaged in heavy training have higher micronutrient needs because they use more energy, lose more minerals through sweat (especially sodium and potassium) and undergo greater physiological stress. Female athletes in endurance sport are particularly vulnerable to iron deficiency because of the combined losses through menstruation and high training volume. A varied, whole-food diet is the recommended way to meet these increased needs — supplementation is not always necessary or effective.

Hydration and the Consequences of Dehydration

Water is the medium in which almost every chemical reaction in the body takes place. Maintaining water balance is critical to performance. Even a 1–2% reduction in body mass through fluid loss can begin to impair sporting performance. Dehydration occurs when the body loses more fluid than it takes in. During intense exercise in warm conditions — such as a cross-country race or a summer football tournament — sweat rates can be high, meaning fluid must be replaced regularly to maintain both performance and safety.

Effects of Dehydration on the Body and Performance

Dehydration triggers a series of interconnected physiological problems. As fluid is lost, blood plasma volume falls and the blood becomes thicker. This increase in blood viscosity means the heart must work harder to push blood around the circulatory system, driving up heart rate. Delivery of oxygen and nutrients to muscles slows, accelerating fatigue. In warm conditions, the body’s ability to shed heat through blood vessels near the skin is also compromised, raising core body temperature and increasing the risk of overheating.

Beyond the cardiovascular effects, dehydration also affects the nervous system. Reaction time slows and decision-making deteriorates — a basketball player who is even mildly dehydrated may make slower, poorer decisions on court. Muscle function degrades too: dehydrated muscles fatigue more rapidly and are more prone to cramping, because the electrolyte balance (sodium, potassium) that enables muscle contraction is disrupted. Staying hydrated before, during and after exercise is therefore a non-negotiable aspect of sports performance for athletes at any level.

A common misconception is that hydration simply means “drink lots.” The key concept is fluid balance — replacing what is lost through sweat, breathing and urine, not overloading the body with fluid. For exam answers, the reward is for understanding the cascade of effects from dehydration: blood plasma falls → blood viscosity rises → heart rate increases → oxygen delivery slows → muscles fatigue and cramp → reaction time slows → decision-making deteriorates. Practise writing that chain in order, anchored to a sporting context.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • A balanced diet contains seven components: carbohydrates (55–60%, main energy source), fats (25–30%, low-intensity energy + insulation), protein (15–20%, muscle growth and repair), plus vitamins, minerals, fibre and water. Carbohydrate is the body’s preferred fuel at all exercise intensities; glycogen stores are the athlete’s key energy reserve.
  • Vitamins and minerals maintain efficient body system function; fibre supports digestion and stable blood glucose; water is the medium for all physiological processes.
  • Dehydration increases blood viscosity, raises heart rate, causes overheating, slows reactions, impairs decision-making and leads to muscle fatigue and cramping — all of which degrade sporting performance at any level.
